title: The Rise of Passive Investing in India: Performance, Risk and Market Efficiency of Index Funds and Actively Managed Mutual Funds
content: Purpose – The paper aims to explore if the speedy migration of Indian investors to index funds/Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs) can be explained by the comparative performance, risk and cost character is tics of passive and active equity mutual funds and how far it is indicative of informational efficiency of Indian equity markets. Design/methodology/approach – AMFI provides industry-level data to us in the AMFI-CRISIL Factbook 2026, combined with the S&P Indices Versus Active (SPIVA) India scorecards for the period ending December 2025. We evaluate performance by benchmark-relative underperformance rates over 1-, 3-, 5- and 10-year horizons, asset- and equal-weighted returns, risk-adjusted comparisons and survivorship. We analyze the evidence through the lens of the Efficient Market Hypothesis, the Grossman-Stiglitz paradox and the Sharpe’s arithmetic of active management and specify a fund-level multi-factor model for replication. Findings – Passive assets reached ~₹13.7 lakh crore by March 2026, increasing industry share of passive from 9.8% to 18.6% in five years. Over 10 years (2006-17), 76.3% of active large cap funds, 82.9% of ELSS funds and 79.0% of mid/small-cap funds underperformed benchmark, and 27% of funds failed to survive a decade. Shorter-horizon findings vary substantially by segment: active mid/small-cap fund beat the benchmark at a high rate in 2025, whereas active large-cap fund failed to do so. The pattern is in line with a near semi-strong-form efficient large cap segment, and a relatively inefficient, illiquid small-cap segment. Originality/value – The article provides fresh, India-specific, 2017 alternative insights on the passive-active debate following SEBI’s move to recategorize the scheme in 2017, and positions the passive growth as an efficiency story not just an investor-cost one.
